newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish police defend anti-riot plastic bullets.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish police defend anti-riot plastic bullets.

text.p: Northern Ireland's police chief defended his force's firing of riot-control plastic bullets on Wednesday after a British police monitoring body urged new safeguards on their use.
Ronnie Flanagan, head of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), told a news conference they had reduced a risk of deaths during sectarian turmoil that swept the province last summer.
"If we had not had at our disposal plastic baton rounds, then the risk to life and damage to property would have been much greater," he told a Belfast news conference.
Since 1972, 16 people have been killed in Northern Ireland in incidents involving plastic bullets, the last in 1989, and more than 500 have been injured.

"What our officers have faced, do face and very sadly what our officers are likely to face in the field of public order is of a totally different character to that faced by our colleagues in Great Britain," Flanagan said.
"They, for example, do not have the risk of terrorists using riots as cover to launch gun and blast bomb attacks."
A report by the Inspector of Constabulary, which monitors the operations of British police forces, had earlier urged the RUC to bring in new safeguards.
The report called the force to think more carefully before issuing plastic bullet guns and to be more willing to refer allegations of their misuse to an independent commission.
The official report said the use of the ammunition was justified in dealing with spontaneous outbreaks of disorder that often occur in the British-ruled province.
The guns used by Northern Ireland police fire 38 mm (1.5 inch) rounds weighing 135 grams (4.8 ounces) that are designed to deliver at a distance the equivalent of a blow from a truncheon.

Introduced in the 1950s, they are potentially lethal but developments over the years to both the weapon and the round have been aimed at making their use as safe as possible, the Inspectorate of Constabulary report said.
But it said the issue of guns that fire plastic ammunition "should be governed by the formal assessment of intelligence and tension indicators".
"There is a risk that in those areas where baton guns are routinely issued, they will be treated as a piece of everyday equipment," it added.

The report said that unlike police forces in England and Wales, the RUC seldom referred incidents in which a policeman was accused of a criminal offence to the Independent Commission for Police Complaints.
"(The) Inspector suggests this should be considered as a reassurance to the public of the thoroughness and impartiality of the investigation," it said.
